source.title: Stress-Testing Capability Elicitation With Password-Locked Models
source.authors: R. Greenblatt; Fabien Roger; D. Krasheninnikov; David Krueger

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests weak-to-strong transfer using password-locked models and correctness rather than the original study’s PGR measurement.
record.gate_note: The claim-relevant result is SFT on Llama7B-generated demonstrations: the authors state that the unlocked models perform above Llama7B but below the password-enabled ceiling. Figure 3 shows the demonstration-count sweeps, but this text does not provide extractable numeric values or PGR calculations. Other SFT results use high-quality demonstrations, not weak labels. The RL results train with rewards rather than weak-model labels, so they are not rows for this claim.
record.test_reason: In §5.1, password-locked 7B models are fine-tuned on demonstrations from a weaker model (Llama7B). The authors state that correctness exceeds Llama7B but stays below the with-password ceiling, and attribute this to weak-to-strong generalization. The student is a password-locked model, a new setting, and the measure is correctness, not PGR. Weak-to-strong is a side result; the paper is about capability elicitation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say Llama7B-demo SFT reaches correctness above Llama7B but below the ceiling, likely due to weak-to-strong generalization, and that this weakens elicitation-by-weaker-demos evaluations. Their main conclusion is about elicitation: a few high-quality demos usually unlock capabilities, and RL works if the weak policy is good enough.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weak-model demonstrations to SFT a stronger model, but first constructs password-locked models and evaluates elicitation by task correctness rather than reporting the original PGR measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and demonstration quality/count affect outcomes; MMLU needs more demonstrations, and weak-model demonstrations produce lower performance than high-quality demonstrations.

fits_no_version.finding: Weak-sample unlocking (B.2): fine-tuning the locked model on a few samples of the same weak policy it was locked to imitate raises correctness in 2/4 tasks. This is a locking artifact, not supervision by a weaker model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning a locked or sandbagging model on samples of its own imitated weak policy can partially restore hidden capability.

record.problems: The weak-to-strong result is described in text but its plotted correctness values are not numerically extractable from this text. PGR is not reported, and the main weak-label comparison uses one named weak supervisor, Llama7B.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded high-quality-demonstration SFT results because their labels are not from a weaker supervisor. Excluded RL results in §6 and Appendix B.3 because they use rewards rather than weak-model labels. Appendix B.2 weak-sample unlocking is not included because the text does not explicitly report those outcomes as beating the weak supervisor.

untested.parts: No confidence loss, ensembling or loss variants applied to weak-label training.
Supervisor and student size are not varied for weak-label SFT. No PGR per task and no analysis of what predicts it. Fig. 8 varies the locking weak policy, not the supervisor.
No exploitation, distribution-shift or error-similarity tests for weak-label training.

missing.what: Overshoot test: student correctness relative to intermediate-supervisor correctness during SFT on Stable Zephyr 2B, Llama 7B and Pythia 3B samples; regular vs adversarial lock.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed to T3 because the student is a password-locked model. V3 links and the V3 limits_scope label were removed: falling below the ceiling (PGR<1) is consistent with the original finding, and task-dependent sample efficiency concerns high-quality demos. B.2 weak-sample unlocking may inflate the above-supervisor gain; the authors say it explains only a small fraction of effects. B.3.2 overshoot results seem to sit uneasily with the §5.1 claim and deserve checking against the figure.

versions.untested_parts: No explicit PGR values are reported; results use correctness comparisons.
Auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling weak supervisors, and the specified weak-label loss variants.
PGR is not calculated; no systematic student-size or representation-predictor analysis of weak-label transfer is reported.
The specified exploits, distribution-shift failures, and shared-error effects are not tested as weak-to-strong failure modes.
No theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor are tested.

source_check.notes: Figure-only entries correctly avoid inventing point estimates. The supplied text is the May 2024 v1 preprint; its later publication classification cannot be verified here.

statements.correction: Table 1 and Figure 3: the four listed 7B student/task combinations; Llama7B-demo SFT exceeds Llama7B correctness but remains below with-password correctness. §4.2: standard errors over 3 seeds. No PGR reported. MMLU uses ground-truth labels as π strong; Figure 7 includes a strongest-model reference, Mistral-7B trained only on ground-truth labels on a distinct training set.
statements.problem: The above-Llama7B result is supported. The blanket assertion that no true-label ceiling is reported overlooks the ground-truth-trained Mistral-7B reference in Figure 7. Publication status is not established by the supplied preprint.

statements.correction: §B.3.2, Figure 15: intermediate-model SFT trajectories on MATH and MMLU; overshoot above convergence correctness occurs only for MATH with Llama 7B and is small. Adversarial locking slightly reduces overshoot. §5.1 and Figure 3: Llama7B-demo SFT exceeds Llama7B itself.
statements.problem: Figure 15 supports rare, small overshoot above convergence correctness, not the claim that elicitation generally stops at the supervisor's own correctness. Converged imitation performance and supervisor performance are different baselines.
